## Definition

The **experimental hypothesis** (H₁ or Hₐ) predicts that the independent variable will have an effect on the dependent variable. It is also called the alternative hypothesis or research hypothesis.

## Key Characteristics

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Predicts effect | States IV will influence DV |
| Testable | Can be supported or refuted by data |
| Based on theory | Derived from existing knowledge |
| Symbol | H₁ or Hₐ |

## Types of Experimental Hypotheses

| Type | Description | Example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| Directional | Specifies direction | "Caffeine will *increase* alertness" |
| Non-directional | Predicts difference only | "Caffeine will *affect* alertness" |

## Writing Hypotheses

A good hypothesis:

1. States the IV and DV clearly
2. Predicts the relationship
3. Is operationalised
4. Is testable

### Example

**Abstract:** "Caffeine affects memory"

**Operationalised:** "Participants who consume 200mg caffeine will recall significantly more words from a 30-word list than participants who consume a placebo."

## Hypothesis Testing Logic

```
State hypotheses
      │
      ▼
H₀: No effect (µ₁ = µ₂)
H₁: Effect exists (µ₁ ≠ µ₂)
      │
      ▼
Collect data
      │
      ▼
Calculate p-value
      │
      ├── p < .05 → Reject H₀, support H₁
      │
      └── p ≥ .05 → Fail to reject H₀
```

## Important Notes

- We never "prove" H₁
- We either reject or fail to reject H₀
- Supporting H₁ means the data are unlikely under H₀
- Non-significant results don't prove H₀ is true
